questions.q: What does "make illegal states unrepresentable" mean in practice?
questions.explain: The goal is to move rules from runtime checks that someone must remember into types the compiler checks everywhere. Runtime checks remain for the rules types cannot express.
options: Validate every object with a schema before saving it
Design the types so that a state the business forbids cannot be built, or cannot be passed where it would do harm
Throw an error whenever an illegal state is detected
Hide illegal states from the user interface

questions.q: Which of these is an invariant of the shop's domain?
questions.explain: An invariant is a rule that must hold for the model at all times. Colours, storage engines and formats are decisions about other layers, not rules of the domain.
options: A refund never exceeds what is left on the captured payment

questions.q: The naive order had status: string, paid: boolean and an optional paymentId. What is the core problem with that design?
questions.explain: A product of independent fields allows every combination. A discriminated union with one interface per state allows exactly the combinations that exist, and ties each piece of data to the state that has it.
options: The fields can combine in ways the business never allows, such as paid: true with no payment id, and nothing ties them together
Optional properties are not allowed in strict mode
A string status cannot be saved in a database

questions.q: Why does the model have no function that takes a PaidOrder and returns a PaidOrder?
questions.explain: Transitions define the allowed moves. markPaid accepts only a PendingOrder, so a paid order cannot be passed to it, and there is no other way to produce a PaidOrder from a paid one.
options: Because interfaces cannot be returned from functions
Because paying again is not a legal move, and if no function can express it, no code can perform it
Because paid orders are frozen at runtime
Because TypeScript forbids functions that return their parameter type

questions.q: payOrder accepts only a PendingOrder. Why can the same order still be paid twice without a version check?
questions.explain: Types cannot express "this value may be used once" or "this value is outdated". Only the store, which sees every request, can refuse the second write, for example with a version check.
options: Two requests can each load the order while it is still pending and each hold a valid PendingOrder; types describe values, not whether they are still current
Because TypeScript does not check function arguments at runtime

questions.q: How does the lesson's VersionedStore refuse the second of two concurrent payments?
questions.explain: Both requests started from version 1 and produced version 2. The first save moves the store to version 2; the second finds 2 where it expected 1 and is refused as stale. This is optimistic concurrency control.
options: It locks the order for 30 seconds
Each transition increments version, and a save succeeds only if the stored version is exactly one less than the new one
It throws when two objects have the same id

questions.q: What is the database equivalent of the version check?
questions.explain: Putting the expected version in the WHERE clause makes the check and the write one atomic statement. Reading first and comparing in code leaves a gap in which another request can write.
options: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1, then compare in code
UPDATE orders SET … WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2, then check that exactly one row changed
A foreign key from payments to orders
DELETE the old row before inserting the new one

questions.q: Which type makes [] a compile error for an order's lines?
questions.explain: A tuple with one required element followed by a rest element needs at least one item. TypeScript reports "Source has 0 element(s) but target requires 1".

questions.q: Why does an OrderLine store unitPrice instead of looking the price up from the product when needed?
questions.explain: Choosing between copying data (a snapshot) and referring to it is a domain decision. Prices on past orders are facts about that moment and must not change with the catalogue.
options: The order must keep the price the customer agreed to, even if the catalogue price changes later
Because branded types cannot refer to other entities

questions.q: Why does newOrder compute total itself instead of taking it as a parameter?
questions.explain: Derived data that is supplied separately can drift from the data it derives from. Computing it in the only constructor removes the possibility.
options: So no caller can create an order whose total disagrees with its lines
Because the total is only needed for display

questions.q: Which rule about refunds does the type of applyRefund(payment: CapturedPayment, …) enforce?
questions.explain: The parameter type encodes the state. The amount rule compares two runtime numbers and is a Result; the permission comes from the use case's permit parameter.
options: The refund amount is at most what is left on the payment
Only a captured payment can be refunded; initiated, failed and fully refunded payments do not fit
The refund is made by finance staff
The refund is recorded in the ledger

questions.q: Why does applyRefund return CapturedPayment | RefundedPayment rather than always a CapturedPayment?
questions.explain: The caller must narrow the result before refunding again. A fully refunded payment then cannot be passed to another refund, which is exactly the rule.
options: To make the return type longer
A partial refund leaves the payment captured, but refunding the rest ends it; the result's state depends on the amount
Because unions are faster to check

questions.q: What stops code outside users.ts from creating a Permit<"payment:refund"> without calling authorize?
questions.explain: An object literal with by and permission is still missing [permitBrand], and nobody outside the module can name that key. A cast could still forge one, which is why casts outside constructors deserve review.
options: The permit is checked against a database
The permit's brand is keyed by a unique symbol that is not exported, so no other module can write an object with that property

questions.q: Why is Permit<"order:pay"> not accepted where Permit<"payment:refund"> is expected?
questions.explain: Parameterising the permit by its permission turns "authorized for something" into "authorized for this". A permit for one operation cannot be reused for another.
options: The brand's type is the permission literal itself, and "order:pay" is not "payment:refund"

questions.q: Ada has the order:pay permission. Why does payOrder still compare permit.by with order.customer?
questions.explain: Role-based permissions answer "may this kind of user do this kind of thing?". Resource rules like ownership depend on the specific record and stay runtime checks inside the use case.
options: It is redundant; the permit already proves it
The role says Ada may pay orders in general; whether she may pay this order depends on its data, which only a runtime check can compare
Because permits do not record a user

questions.q: Why do the use cases return their events instead of publishing them directly?
questions.explain: A pure use case returns everything that happened: new states, events and ledger transactions. The shell saves and publishes them, ideally in the same database transaction.
options: Publishing is not possible in TypeScript
The functions stay pure and testable, and the events are part of the result type, so the shell cannot ignore that they exist

questions.q: Why is "debits equal credits" enforced by the transaction() smart constructor and not by a type?
questions.explain: Types can say "a non-empty list of entries", but not "whose amounts sum to zero". A constructor checks the sums once and brands the result, so every function that accepts a Transaction can trust it.
options: Because ledgers are stored in a database
It is a rule about the sum of a list of runtime numbers, which no type can compute
Because brands cannot be used on objects

questions.q: Why does transaction() throw on unbalanced entries instead of returning a Result?
questions.explain: Expected failures caused by users belong in the return type; programming errors should fail loudly. A ledger that does not balance means the code is wrong.
options: The entries are built by our own code, so an unbalanced transaction is a bug, not an expected user mistake

questions.q: Which tool fits the rule "this payment belongs to this order"?
questions.explain: The rule relates two values that exist only at runtime. Types can require a captured payment and a pending order; whether they belong together must be compared.

questions.q: What does a database CHECK constraint such as "status = 'paid' implies payment_id IS NOT NULL" add to the model?
questions.explain: Types protect only code that is type-checked with your model. The database is shared, so mirroring the union's rules there keeps illegal rows out regardless of who writes them.
options: Nothing; the TypeScript types already guarantee it
It enforces the same rule for every writer, including scripts, migrations and other services that never see your types
It replaces the need to parse rows

questions.q: A repository reads a row with status = 'paid' and payment_id = NULL. What should it do?
questions.explain: The repository is a boundary, like a request handler. It parses rows into the precise union and refuses rows that no state allows, so corrupt data is noticed where it enters the program.
options: Return a PaidOrder with paymentId: null as never
Report the row as corrupt instead of producing a half-valid order

questions.q: Why keep API response types (DTOs) separate from the domain types?
questions.explain: If the response type is the domain type, every internal change (a new state, a renamed field) breaks clients. A mapper at the edge absorbs those changes.
options: The API is a public contract that must stay stable, while domain types change with the business; mapping at the edge lets each evolve on its own

questions.q: Where does illegal-state modelling pay off least?
questions.explain: The technique costs types, constructors and transitions. It pays for itself where mistakes cost money or trust, not for simple settings with no rules.

questions.q: A type test reads // @ts-expect-error above refundPayment(payPermit, failedPayment, …). Why is it a weak test?
questions.explain: The directive only checks that some error occurs. Keep exactly one mistake per expected error, so the test fails when that one rule is lost.
options: The line has two errors (wrong permit and failed payment); if failed payments became refundable, the permit error alone would keep the test passing
Because the function is never called
Because type tests cannot test parameters

questions.q: The use cases never read the clock; at timestamps are passed in. Why?
questions.explain: The clock is a hidden input. Passing time in (from the shell) is the functional core, imperative shell idea applied to a whole domain.
options: It keeps the domain pure: the same function behaves the same in tests, request handlers and queue workers
Because Date is not available in TypeScript

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: At runtime a non-empty tuple is an ordinary array. The type guarantees that lines[0] exists, so it is typed string, not string | undefined.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each transition builds a new object, so the pending order is untouched and each step adds one to the version. Spread keeps the original key order, and new keys are added at the end.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both a and b were derived from version 1. Whichever saves first wins; the other is stale. The shipping change, derived from the saved version 2, then succeeds.
options:
saved v1
saved v2 stale (found 2) saved v3

saved v1
saved v2 saved v2 saved v3

saved v1
saved v2 stale (found 2) stale (found 2)

saved v1
stale (found 1) stale (found 1) saved v3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After refunding 320,000, 1,700,000 is left: more is refused, exactly the rest ends the payment. The final state is built fresh, so the refunded counter of a captured payment does not linger.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A user has the union of their roles' permissions. A customer alone cannot refund; a customer who is also in finance can; a user with no roles can do nothing.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A transaction may have more than two entries; only the totals per side must match. The second has a typo (one zero missing), which the check catches: 320,000 − 32,000 = 288,000.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Spread copies every property, including ones that belong only to the old state. Building the final state explicitly leaves the partial-refund counter behind, so the stored object matches its type exactly.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 2,020,000 + 60,000 − 320,000 = 1,760,000. Checking type narrows each event, so amount is only read on events that have it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Reflect.set reports whether a write succeeded; on a frozen object it fails and the permit keeps its user. A spread copy is a new, unfrozen object; in TypeScript it would also lose the permit's brand, so it could not be passed where a Permit is required.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The parser accepts only rows that match a state exactly. "Paid" with a capital letter is not "paid", and a paid row without a payment id is refused instead of becoming a half-valid order.
options: paid by PAY-88 | corrupt: paid without payment | corrupt: unknown status Paid
paid by PAY-88 | paid by null | paid by PAY-9
paid by PAY-88 | corrupt: paid without payment | paid by PAY-9
paid by PAY-88 | pending | corrupt: unknown status Paid

questions.q: Finish cancel(order, reason): it only accepts a pending order, returns a cancelled order with the reason and the version increased by one, and leaves the original untouched. The program should print pending 1 cancelled 2 out of stock.
questions.explain: The parameter type is the rule: only pending orders can be cancelled. Returning a new object keeps the old state intact, and the version bump lets the store detect a concurrent change.

questions.q: Finish applyRefund: refuse 0 and anything above what is left; a refund of exactly what is left returns a fresh refunded payment (no refunded field); otherwise return the captured payment with refunded increased. The program should print captured 320000 | exceeds 1700000 | refunded | nothing.
questions.explain: The type restricts refunds to captured payments; the function enforces the amount rules that depend on runtime numbers. The order of checks matters: zero first, then the upper bound, then "exactly the rest".

questions.q: Finish authorize(user, permission): return a frozen permit { by, permission } if any of the user's roles grants the permission, otherwise undefined. The program should print USR-3 payment:refund | denied | USR-5 order:ship.
questions.explain: The as readonly Permission[] widens one role's literal tuple so includes accepts any permission. In the lesson the permit also carries a symbol brand, so only this function can create one.

questions.q: Finish transaction(memo, entries): throw a RangeError when the debits do not equal the credits, otherwise return a frozen { memo, entries }. The program should print refund on PAY-88 true | RangeError.
questions.explain: The non-empty tuple type guarantees at least one entry; only the constructor can guarantee the sums match. Freezing keeps a checked transaction from being changed afterwards.

questions.q: Finish shipAll: from a list of orders in mixed states, ship every paid order (status "shipped", a tracking code GIG- plus its position in the list, version plus one) and leave the others unchanged. The program should print shipped:GIG-0 pending shipped:GIG-2 cancelled.
questions.explain: Inside the ternary, order is narrowed to the paid member, so the spread has a paymentId and the result fits the shipped member. Only paid orders are transformed; the others pass through as the same objects.

questions.q: Finish parseRow: turn a database row into an order state, or an error string. pending needs nothing; paid needs payment_id; cancelled needs cancel_reason; anything else is an unknown status. The program should print pending | paid PAY-88 | ORD-3: paid without payment_id | ORD-4: unknown status "archived".
questions.explain: The row type is honest about what the database can hold; the parser is the one place that turns it into the precise union, and it names the row and the problem when the data does not fit any state.
questions.expected: pending | paid PAY-88 | ORD-3: paid without payment_id | ORD-4: unknown status "archived"

questions.q: Finish balances: from a list of ledger transactions, compute each account's balance (debits add, credits subtract) and return them sorted by account name. The program should print bank:1700000 refunds:320000 sales:-2020000 total:0.
questions.explain: Because every transaction was balanced when it was created, the balances of all accounts always sum to zero. That total is a cheap health check to run on the whole ledger.
